Europe Home page Europe 0 0 Euractiv: EU member states lift ban on imports of Russian sable fur 27 July 2026 11:13 (UTC +04:00) Imports of luxury Russian sable pelts may resume after EU member states lifted a ban that had only been introduced in April, Euractiv said, Ukrainska Pravda reports. The change was included in the latest package of EU sanctions against Russia agreed by Brussels last week. The European Commission justified the exemption by arguing that Russia dominates the global trade in sable pelts, leaving European manufacturers with very few alternative suppliers. "Apparently, it's very difficult to get them anywhere else," a senior EU official said. Italy and Greece, the two largest buyers of Russian sable pelts within the EU, pushed for the exemption, a European diplomat told the outlet. The sable is a small carnivorous mammal native to the forests of northern Asia. It is prized for its exceptionally soft fur and has long been sought after by Europe's luxury fashion houses. Russian sable coats can sell for tens or even hundreds of thousands of euros. According to Sojuzpushnina, Russia's only international fur auction house, Greek and Italian companies continue to rank among the leading international buyers of the fur, alongside Chinese and Russian firms. For example, Italian fur manufacturer Maurizio Braschi purchased the most expensive lot of sable at auction in September 2022 on behalf of Braschi, and again in May 2023 for a private client in Moscow, according to publicly available records from Sojuzpushnina. Meanwhile, imports of finished fur garments into the EU and exports of such products to Russia remain prohibited under sanctions introduced in 2022, alongside other luxury goods such as diamonds and caviar. In 2022, fur producers in Greece strongly opposed those sanctions, warning that they would amount to a death sentence for the industry. The exemption agreed last week restores access to raw Russian sable pelts, although exports of finished fur garments to Russia remain banned. The policy change comes as Brussels continues to consider the future of its own fur farming industry. An EU-wide ban on fur farming is being considered following a successful European Citizens' Initiative calling for an end to the practice across the EU as well as a ban on the import and sale of fur products. Only a handful of EU countries, including Spain, Greece, Hungary, Finland and Poland, still have fur farms in operation, although Poland has already adopted legislation to phase out the industry over the coming years. However, the European Commission has repeatedly postponed its decision, which had originally been expected in March. A draft proposal suggested that the Commission favours strengthening animal welfare standards instead of introducing a complete ban on fur production and import. Jukes and James Orr, the party’s head of policy, were recorded apparently plotting to bypass electoral laws. Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Reuters View image in fullscreen Nigel Farage, the Reform leader, and his adviser Dan Jukes arrive at the Clacton byelection in August. Jukes and James Orr, the party’s head of policy, were recorded apparently plotting to bypass electoral laws. Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Reuters Reform UK Investigations launched into polling firm at centre of Reform UK allegations British Polling Council and Market Research Society announce inquiries into JL Partners, which has been accused of breaking transparency rules What is the latest finance scandal facing Reform UK? Geraldine McKelvie Fri 4 Sep 2026 12.14 EDT Last modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 14.11 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A polling firm at the centre of allegations that Reform UK breached electoral law is being investigated by two industry bodies. JL Partners, which is run by former Conservative aides, has been accused of breaking transparency rules by failing to declare that three separate polls had been commissioned by the party. The company is a member of the British Polling Council and the Market Research Society, who say the identity of a client commissioning a poll should be disclosed when the results enter the public domain. Both organisations confirmed on Friday that they had launched inquiries into JL Partners. The reviews have come after Channel 4 News broadcast footage gathered by undercover reporters during a year-long investigation into Reform’s finances on Thursday night. Investigative journalists from Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a Reform donor and his American father, who paid for more than £30,000 of polling from JL Partners that generated positive headlines for the party. Nigel Farage, the party leader, was filmed saying the polling was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck”. In the footage, Farage appeared to welcome the suggestion of a larger donation to the party. He was told the UK-based son could be registered as the official donor, despite the money originating from his father. Farage said: “Both of you, thank you.” 11:20 Reform donations scandal: is this the final blow for Farage? - The Latest In the UK, only those registered on the electoral roll are permitted to donate to political parties, meaning the polls and the proposed larger donation could both be classed as illegal. On Friday, as its annual conference got under way in Birmingham, Reform said it had suspended two senior officials who were filmed as part of the Channel 4 News investigation. James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, a senior adviser to Farage, were both recorded apparently plotting to bypass electoral laws. The first poll, conducted in January, related to the Labour government’s aborted plans to cancel some local elections, which Reform strongly opposed. The poll indicated Labour would face heavy defeats if these went ahead. The second, published in April, suggested that two-thirds of voters wanted the then prime minister, Keir Starmer, to resign. The third, released in June, appeared to show that support for Reform among trade union members was drawing level with Labour. JL Partners’ co-founder James Johnson was covertly filmed discussing the Reform polling, telling one of the reporters that his company had done “a little bit of informal rule-bending” in relation to one survey. He admitted that it “should have disclosed who the client was” when publishing the data. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion The results of the polling appeared on the front pages of the Times and the Daily Telegraph. Both newspapers said they had not been aware that the polling had been commissioned by Reform. The British Polling Council said on Friday that “all data and research findings made on the basis of social or political polls conducted in the United Kingdom … must include reference to the client commissioning the survey”. It added that it was clear its rules had been breached in relation to the polls paid for by Reform. “According to the programme, this may have been deliberate,” a spokesperson added. “We are seeking further information from the BPC member concerned and expect them to make information available after further consideration.” The Market Research Society said: “MRS is aware of the Channel 4 reporting involving an MRS Company Partner. The matter is being referred to the Market Research Standards Board (MRSB) for review in line with its established complaint procedures.” JL Partners told Channel 4 News: “Despite there being no concern about the accuracy of our work, the report did reveal weaknesses in our procedures. For that reason JL Partners is reviewing those procedures in order to eliminate possible grey areas and ambiguities and strengthen our safeguards for the future.” The company did not respond to follow-up queries from the Guardian. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Protest called by Daphne Caruana Galizia's family and civic movements outside the office of the prime minister in Valletta, Malta, 29 November 2019. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Protest called by Daphne Caruana Galizia's family and civic movements outside the office of the prime minister in Valletta, Malta, 29 November 2019. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Opinion Daphne Caruana Galizia Nine years after Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, Europe must finally address Malta’s culture of impunity Pieter Omtzigt and Emanuel Delia Much of the corruption exposed by this brave woman remains unpunished. Brussels must carry on her work and demand reform Thu 10 Sep 2026 04.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 04.53 EDT Share N ine years ago, Daphne Caruana Galizia, Malta’s foremost investigative journalist, was assassinated by a car bomb outside her home. The men who carried out the killing have been convicted or admitted their involvement. Nobody has been convicted of commissioning her murder. Last week, a jury acquitted Yorgen Fenech, one of Malta’s most prominent businessmen, of complicity in the assassination and criminal association. We have followed this case from different places: one of us from Malta, as a journalist and civil society activist campaigning for accountability after Daphne’s assassination; the other served as the Council of Europe’s rapporteur scrutinising the investigation and Malta’s failures of the rule of law. We were shocked by the verdict, but we respect it. The jurors decided, by eight votes to one, that Fenech’s guilt had not been proved beyond reasonable doubt. We are not asking for their verdict to be disregarded or reversed by political pressure. But the verdict does not erase what the trial exposed. Fenech admitted that he knew of the murder plan before Daphne was killed and that, while the plan was still live, he gave €50,000 to Melvin Theuma , the middleman who recruited the killers. Fenech said the money was intended to reimburse Theuma for money already paid and to persuade him to stop the assassination. He also admitted he passed confidential information about the police investigation to Theuma and gave him further sums of money. He told the court he was blackmailed by Theuma. But Fenech denied commissioning or financing the murder. His explanation was that he had been acting out of misplaced loyalty to Keith Schembri, then chief of staff to Malta’s prime minister and one of his closest friends. The picture is appalling. A businessman at the heart of Malta’s economic establishment, the prime minister’s closest aide and the man organising the murder of the country’s most prominent investigative journalist were moving within the same small circle. Daphne had spent the last years of her life investigating precisely this proximity between political power, private wealth and people willing to operate outside the law. The Maltese government itself commissioned an independent public inquiry into her assassination. It concluded in 2021 that the state had created a culture of impunity and an atmosphere in which her murder became possible. Five years later, most of its recommendations remain unimplemented. Nor has there been anything approaching adequate accountability for the corruption Daphne was investigating. There are uncomfortable precedents. In Russia, people were convicted for their roles in the murders of journalist Anna Politkovskaya and opposition politician Boris Nemtsov. But the European court of human rights found that the authorities had failed adequately to identify and pursue those who actually commissioned the killings. Malta is not Russia, but it is the case that convicting the people who carried out a murder cannot be the end of the state’s responsibility if whoever commissioned the crime remains unidentified and unpunished. This should concern Brussels as much as Valletta. View image in fullscreen Yorgen Fenech after being found not quilty of the murder of Daphne Caruana Galizia, 2 September 2026. Photograph: Matthew Mirabelli/AFP/Getty Images Malta’s failures do not stop at its coastline. A licence to conduct business in Malta, with limited government supervision, is effectively a licence to conduct business across the European Union . Weak enforcement in one member state creates opportunities throughout the union. This is why impunity in Malta is not merely a Maltese problem. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion On Wednesday, the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe (Pace) returned formally to Daphne’s case. Its committee on legal affairs and human rights heard evidence from Daphne’s son Matthew Caruana Galizia and her sister Corinne Vella. Shami Chakrabarti, the committee’s rapporteur, is preparing a new report, entitled Justice delayed: the unfinished implementation of the Daphne Caruana Galizia case. Her mandate includes examining the implementation of the public inquiry’s recommendations and Malta’s compliance with Council of Europe standards on the rule of law and press freedom. The timing could hardly be more important. Even Pace’s own monitoring committee, while recognising reforms undertaken since 2019, concluded that they addressed only part of the deficiencies and that comprehensive reform of Malta’s democratic institutions and system of checks and balances remained necessary. Malta’s prime minister, Robert Abela, should meet Chakrabarti at the earliest opportunity and give her work the Maltese government’s full cooperation. But the Council of Europe should go further. Pace has a monitoring committee specifically charged with examining whether member states are meeting their obligations to democracy, human rights and the rule of law. Malta has already been examined by that committee, which raised concerns about corruption, checks and balances, parliamentary oversight and the continuing culture of impunity. The events of the past week strengthen the case for renewed, comprehensive scrutiny of the state of the rule of law in Malta. Sabotage, leaks and political ties: the story of the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trial Read more Europe owes something to Daphne and to her family, who have spent nearly nine years fighting for truths the state should have established without requiring their persistence. But there is also a matter of European self-interest. The EU and the Council of Europe cannot afford pockets within their borders where serious corruption goes unpunished and political and economic power can frustrate accountability. The jury has decided that the prosecution did not prove Yorgen Fenech criminally responsible for Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder. That judgment must be respected. It cannot become an answer to everything else. Nearly nine years after Daphne was assassinated, nobody has been convicted of ordering her murder. Much of the corruption she exposed remains unpunished. Most of the reforms recommended by the public inquiry remain undone. It is high time for Europe to start paying attention again. Pieter Omtzigt is a former Dutch MP who served as the Council of Europe parliamentary assembly’s rapporteur on the assassination of Daphne Caruana Galizia and the rule of law in Malta. Emanuel Delia is a Maltese journalist and co-founder of Repubblika, a civil society organisation campaigning for rule of law and accountability in Malta Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? https://astanatimes.com/2026/09/kazakhst.text: Tuesday, 13 October, 2026 Almaty 61 °F / 16 °C Astana 50 °F / 10 °C All Stories Nation Astana Culture Sports People Kazakhstan Regions State of the Nation Election 2022 Election 2023 International Astana International Forum Kazakhstan’s Presidency in SCO 5th World Nomad Games Business Central Asia Opinions All Stories Nation Astana Culture Sports People Kazakhstan Regions State of the Nation Election 2022 Election 2023 International Astana International Forum Kazakhstan’s Presidency in SCO 5th World Nomad Games Business Central Asia Opinions Kazakhstan’s University Offensive By Alexander Dergay in Editor’s Picks , Opinions on 29 September 2026 Germany’s future in Central Asia’s boom market will be decided in the lecture hall Kazakhstan is the gateway to a growth region, yet Germany lacks knowledge of it. Those who invest in talent gain networks and markets. Those who wait fall behind. Berlin needs to act. On Monday, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has arrived in Germany. Interest is high, since Kazakhstan is becoming one of Germany’s most important economic partners. Knowledge about the country has barely kept pace. Some would call it typically German. We discover new markets, debate billion-euro projects and know surprisingly little about the countries behind them. Alexander Dergay. In 2025, the country accounted for more than 80 percent of German trade with Central Asia. The country is evolving from a commodity supplier into a production location and logistics hub, and it is the gateway to a market of more than 80 million people. Yet who in Germany knows Kazakh universities, companies and institutions? Who speaks the languages, has studied there or has built networks over years? Very few. In Kazakhstan, this gap is increasingly becoming a competitive disadvantage. Too few German students spend extended time in the country, university partnerships remain limited and personal networks are thin. The result is a shortage of people who know the market from first-hand experience, beyond presentations and statistics. An analysis by Boston Consulting Group (BCG) shows how far the region’s economic weight has already shifted. In the paper “Why Investors Are Turning to Central Asia and Caspian,” published in September 2025, the authors examine the investment potential of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan and the Kyrgyz Republic. Together, the four states have around 70 million inhabitants and an economic output of about $440 billion. Kazakhstan accounts for almost 60 percent of regional GDP. The study also highlights the region’s comparatively well-educated labor pool, with almost seven million workers holding a university degree and a further 11.5 million with vocational or equivalent qualifications. Konstantin Polunin, the director and partner at BCG and one of the study’s authors, summarized the development to this newspaper last year. “What we are seeing is a lasting structural change,” he said. “Germany underestimates this potential,” Kanat Kozhakhmet, the president of Narxoz University in Almaty, told this newspaper. “Cooperation between Kazakh and German universities has so far been clearly insufficient.” In his view, universities, internships, research and skilled-worker programs belong much closer to the center of economic relations. “We need to build a roadmap for cooperation,” he said. Founded in 1963, Narxoz University is one of the nation’s long-established economics universities. For German partners, Kozhakhmet sees potential in joint study and practical programs, resource research, technology projects and the training of technical specialists. Kazakhstan sends its students into the world His criticism concerns the reach of German universities, whose quality he does not question. German universities, he said, are barely visible at Kazakh schools, at education agencies and in the networks through which families organize study abroad. Other countries have courted young talent more actively for years. Whoever reaches these students builds ties to a generation that will later work in companies, ministries, state corporations and academia. According to UNESCO data, around 91,200 Kazakhs study abroad. Germany counts 126,400, with a population roughly 4.5 times larger. This places Kazakhstan among the countries with the largest outbound student flows worldwide. Around 59,000 Kazakhs studied in Russia in 2021. China now counts more than 11,000 Kazakh students, and other published estimates exceed 14,000. Figures on the state Bolashak scholarship program show how strongly Astana treats education as a strategic investment in competitive talent. Over 33 years, more than 13,200 specialists have been trained abroad. Today, 45 percent of alumni work in the private sector or as entrepreneurs, 25 percent in state structures and 18 percent in national companies. Of the Bolashak and academic stays abroad reported for 2024/25, 57.3 percent went to the USA, 29 percent to the United Kingdom and 4.6 percent to Germany. For a country whose higher education system enjoys a strong international reputation, this is a small share. Germany also falls short of its potential in academic mobility. In 2024, 792 Kazakh students went to Türkiye and 691 to Poland. Germany attracted 193. This stands out because German universities are growing internationally, with around 420,000 foreign students and doctoral candidates expected for the 2025/26 winter semester. According to available data, only about one in 220 international students comes from Kazakhstan. An internationally successful higher education location is therefore tapping only a small part of the potential in a country with a strong orientation toward study abroad. Kazakhstan becomes an education hub itself At the same time, Kazakhstan is changing from a source country of mobile students into a regional higher education location. In the 2025/26 academic year, around 35,000 foreign students from 88 countries were enrolled. The government is building a network of international branch campuses and partnerships, with more than 30 projects at various stages of development. The United Kingdom and Türkiye show how such relationships can grow. More than 5,700 Kazakhs have studied in the UK on Bolashak scholarships alone. Cardiff University opened its first campus abroad in Astana, which is also the first campus of a Russell Group university in Central Asia. Türkiye works through the jointly run Khoja Akhmet Yassawi University in Turkistan, a large scholarship program and closer links between study and business practice. Within a decade, the number of international students in Türkiye rose from around 72,000 to more than 340,000. Germany has a network, though a small one The German-Kazakh University in Almaty has around 700 students, nine bachelor’s and five master’s programs, and hosts about 20 German guest lecturers per semester. Anhalt University of Applied Sciences is present in Almaty. At Yessenov University in Aktau, programs in logistics, energy and environmental engineering, and mechatronics run with German participation. The Goethe-Institut’s PASCH network includes eight schools, 20 teachers and around 2,600 pupils. DAAD, GIZ, the Goethe-Institut, the AHK, political foundations and German companies add to this. Mobility remains low despite this base. In 2025, the DAAD funded a total of 942 people from Kazakhstan and 141 people from Germany traveling to Kazakhstan. Of the 114 Germans in project funding, 105 spent a month or less in the country. Individual funding went to 11, and 9 of them stayed longer than six months. Kazakh authorities cite around 2,000 students from Kazakhstan in Germany, compared with a few dozen German citizens at Kazakh universities. In Aktau, an Institute for Sustainable Engineering has been established with German support, including stays at German partner universities. Beyond that, a dense network of academic contacts exists. In 2023, both governments already pointed to 178 university agreements. The figure, however, says little about the depth of cooperation. Double-degree programs illustrate this. At the end of 2023, universities offered 181 such programs with foreign partners. Of these, 102 ran with Russian universities, 12 with Poland, 10 with Germany and 9 with France. Germany has an established academic presence in the country, yet has so far left the potential of more institutionalized partnerships largely unused. Skills shortages make education an economic issue The AHK survey of German companies in Central Asia gives the topic an immediate economic dimension. In the World Business Outlook of spring 2025, shortages of skilled workers and economic policy conditions were among the companies’ main concerns. Around 64 percent of the companies surveyed were based in Kazakhstan. Qualified staff are in demand particularly in energy, construction, telecommunications and IT. At the same time, Kazakhstan wants to keep more processing and technological value creation in the country. Mining, energy, mechanical engineering, logistics and digitalization need engineers, mechatronics technicians, IT specialists, laboratory staff and environmental technology experts. Germany brings machinery, industrial experience and a strong vocational training system. Universities are expanding technical programs. Both can be linked directly to investment projects. “Kazakhstan in Practice” A German approach can build on existing structures. With “Russia in Practice,” the DAAD already had a format that combined study with everyday business life. German students and graduates went to companies on site for six months, and the DAAD financed the scholarship, travel, insurance and, where needed, language courses. The same basic idea could be relaunched for Central Asia, with longer stays, a company or research institution as practice partner, language support and a clear link to the degree program. “Kazakhstan in Practice” or “Central Asia in Practice” could bring young German experts to industrial and resource regions, logistics specialists to Aktau and the Middle Corridor, computer scientists to digital projects and economists to companies or universities. Narxoz would be a partner in Almaty. Kozhakhmet wants to link such formats more closely with companies and points to resource research, technology and engineering training as fields for new cooperation. For Polunin, the education question continues an economic development that began with growing international interest in Central Asia. “We pointed out last year that the rise of Central Asia is a lasting structural change,” he told this newspaper. “Today the question is whether the capital the region attracts can be turned into real capabilities. That requires human capital, research, training and technology. Kazakhstan has the opportunity to position itself as an economic gateway and increasingly also as the education and science hub of Central Asia. For Germany, this opens the possibility of thinking about economic cooperation, talent development and research much more closely together,” Polunin added. Many individual projects could thus become a joint strategy. Kozhakhmet’s idea of an education roadmap would build on structures that already exist. If new industrial projects are agreed during the presidential visit, the staffing question can be addressed at the same time, from the university in Almaty to the German company on the Middle Corridor. The author is Alexander Dergay, the founder and managing partner of Orbis Nova, a research and analysis firm. Dergay is also cooperating with geopolitical foresight agency Nightingale Int. He worked for several years as an adviser and analyst specializing in geostrategic risk before serving as an foreign policy editor at the Berliner Zeitung and the Ostdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung, Germany. Beállítom Egy pétervásárai nő azt mondta, azért lett lakhatatlan a háza, mert kigyulladt a frissen vásárolt, keveset használt elektromos rollere. Kiss Réka állította az RTL Híradónak , hogy a rollert mindössze két héttel azelőtt vette, hogy az kigyulladt volna, pedig ő betartotta a tárolási és töltési szabályokat. Három kilométert sem ment az új rollerrel, amit még azért kapott ajándékba, mert fájt a lába – mondta a pétervásárai nő. Június 10-én épp a szomszédban volt, amikor hallotta, hogy ugatnak a kutyái. Mire hazaért, már gomolygott a füst a házából. Ahogy bejutott, látta, hogy lángol a kanapé az egyik szobában. A szakértők a tűz eloltása után megállapították, hogy zárlatos volt a roller, ezért kapott lángra. Kiss Réka azt mondta, használat előtt figyelmesen elolvasta a használati útmutatót, mindent szabályosan csinált. A roller forgalmazója eddig 250 ezer forintot fizetett neki, a biztosítója kifizette az ingóságok értékét. Viszont úgy érzi, ezzel nem térítették meg az összes kárt, amit az eset okozott neki. Kiss Réka egy Facebook-posztban arról írt, ügyvédet keres , mert peres úton akarja elérni, hogy teljes kártérítést kapjon a rollert gyártó cégtől. Azt írta, az otthonukban tárolt elektromos roller júniusban magától kigyulladt, pedig „nem állt töltés alatt, egyszerűen a szobában volt”.
